name: The Pax Mongolica, Safe Passage Across Asia
summary: At the height of Mongol dominance, a merchant with a paiza (Mongol safe-conduct tablet) could travel from China to Hungary in relative safety. The Mongol postal relay system (yam), universal commercial protection, and standardized weights enabled unprecedented long-distance trade. Friar John of Plano Carpini (1245), William of Rubruck (1253), and Marco Polo (1271-95) all make transcontinental journeys impossible before or after this brief window.

_quarry.structural_significance: The Pax Mongolica is a historically unique episode of transcontinental connectivity; its commercial integration facilitates the technology transfers (gunpowder, paper, printing) that transform Europe; its biological integration enables the Black Death (Y. pestis travels from Central Asian rodent reservoirs to the Black Sea coast via the trade routes); the Pax ends with the dissolution of Mongol unity in the 1340s-1360s
